analysis.one_liner: Transfers the U.S. Postal Service to a private corporation at no charge.
analysis.headline: A bill to hand the Postal Service to a private corporation — with two cosponsors — died in a House subcommittee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have abolished the U.S. Postal Service as a public institution and turned all of its property over to a new private corporation — and required that the corporation pay nothing for those assets. The corporation's first stock could be issued only to postal employees during a one-year window, and a Presidential commission would manage the handoff. The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in a House subcommittee until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: The people who would incorporate the new company (up to nine individuals chosen in a postal-employee election) would take control of every USPS asset and pay nothing for it. Postal employees who bought stock during the first year would become shareholder-owners, and the bill promises their retirement benefits would stay comparable. Long term, the shareholders of a private mail monopoly — protected from competitors by the private express statutes for its first five years — would gain the most, since the bill requires only recommendations, not guarantees, on how postal rates would be set after that.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The new corporation's owners and employee-shareholders

how_it_helps.text: Transfers every asset of the Postal Service to a private corporation and explicitly requires that no payment be made for those assets — a public enterprise handed over for free.
Lets the corporation issue stock only to postal employees for the first year, giving workers a chance at ownership, with a Postal Privatization Commission deciding how shares are issued.
Promises transferred postal workers retirement benefits comparable to what they would have earned under USPS.
Continues the private express statutes — the laws that make first-class mail a legal monopoly — for the new corporation's first five years, shielding it from competition while it gets established.

analysis.who_pays: The public. Every USPS asset — buildings, vehicles, networks, and the legal monopoly on first-class mail — would be transferred without any payment to the government. After a five-year window in which the President merely proposes how postage rates would be set, customers in high-cost areas would depend on a private monopoly's choices; universal service and uniform rates are stated as purposes but not guaranteed terms. Postal workers would trade public-employee status and job protections for private employment, keeping stock and comparable pensions but little else.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public, giving away USPS for nothing

drawbacks.text: The public would permanently lose the Postal Service and all its assets without receiving anything in return; the bill forbids any payment for the transferred property.

Rate-setting and universal-service obligations are left to the new corporation's stated purposes and to recommendations the President would make, not enforceable guarantees — after the five-year monopoly protection, nothing in the bill ensures affordable uniform rates or service to rural and high-cost areas.

The Postal Privatization Commission that runs the handoff would have nine members chosen by the President, with only two required to represent employee interests — workers would have little say over the terms of their own company's creation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The employee-ownership feature and the comparable-pension promise are real sweeteners, but they do not change the core transaction: a self-funding public service with a universal-service mission would be given away free to a private monopoly, with its rate rules left to future recommendations rather than firm law. On its own terms, the bill's costs to the public and to postal workers as employees far outweigh the stock that workers could buy in year one.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to a House subcommittee a few days after introduction and stayed there, never getting a hearing or a vote, until that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Philip Crane introduced the bill on July 22, 1999, joined by Reps. Dana Rohrabacher and Christopher Cox.
The House referred it to the Committee on Government Reform the same day, and on July 26, 1999 it went to the Subcommittee on Postal Service.
No further action of any kind was taken — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Postal Service and its employees kept their public status, and the public kept a public asset that the bill would have transferred for free. No private party gained anything because the bill never advanced.

against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed privatization of the Postal Service during this era, though the record shows no specific action on this bill.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the only recorded positions are the three Republican sponsors, and no one else acted on the bill.

industries.industry: The new private postal corporation and its incorporators
industries.note: The bill would create a private mail monopoly and hand it every USPS asset without payment, with the private express statutes protecting it from competitors for five years. Ordinary mail customers would face a private company deciding rates and service levels with only provisional oversight.

industries.industry: Private delivery carriers (parcel and express services)
industries.note: Privatization would eventually open the postal market, but for the first five years the private express statutes would keep the new corporation's monopoly intact, delaying competition. Over time, carriers could gain access to a market now dominated by a private rival.

Workers could buy stock in the new company during a one-year window and are promised comparable retirement benefits, but they would lose public-employee status and the job protections that come with it. Only two of nine commission members would represent their interests during the transfer.
